# Hydration and Evidence Fitting {#sec-hydration}

Retrieval (@sec-retrieval) selects a ranked set of memories, 11 at neutral
knobs. Hydration then turns each selection into evidence. It loads the
memory's payloads and attaches the context a person would recall around the
hit. Finally it fits the whole packet to the caller's budget. Hydration never
changes the ranking, the pool, or the number of retrieved memories, and it
runs only after selection, so its cost follows the packet rather than the
store.

## Packet Structure

A query's `Context` carries three blocks:

* `standing_memory`: the standing block (@sec-retrieval). It holds at most 5
  directive signals within 2 KiB and is not counted in the retrieved top-k.
* `retrieved_memory`: the ranked memories. Each has its own payloads plus attached
  blobs (adjacent turns, superseded predecessors, superseding successors).
* `working_memory`: the active slots in insertion order (@sec-advanced).

Every retrieved memory exposes `content` (one entry per blob),
`content_mimetypes` and `content_timestamps`, index-aligned. A memory that
holds signals of several modalities has modality `"mixed"` and returns every
payload with its own MIME type. Earlier builds took a majority vote, which
dropped minority-modality payloads.

## Contiguity Hydration

Recalling one moment of a conversation brings back what was said around it.
This is the temporal-contiguity effect of episodic recall, and it fades with
distance. A retrieved turn is rarely self-contained: a question's answer, the
statement an acknowledgement refers to, or the user message a reply was
written for usually sits one or two turns away. For each of the top 11
anchors, the engine attaches adjacent turns as extra blobs of the anchor:

```text
neighbours(anchor) = adjacent LONG_TERM rows in write order
                     within 16 ids and 30 minutes of the anchor,
                     same source stream, any modality,
                     not hidden by a correction from the same stretch
pass 1 (lag 1): for anchors in rank order: successor, then predecessor
pass 2 (lag 2): with what budget is left, the turns two steps away
charge: text clipped to 480 B; other media 480 B each
budget: 12 KiB per context
```

Forward association is stronger than backward, so the successor (usually the
reply) is attached first.

* **Clip window.** Text is clipped on a UTF-8 boundary. The first 64 bytes
  (the turn header: time, speaker) stay, followed by the 480-byte window that
  covers the most distinct query terms.
* **Cost.** All lag-1 probes run in one statement and all lag-2 probes in
  another. Each probe is a primary-key range lookup plus one indexed
  supersession check.
* **Interaction with retrieval.** Neighbour deferral (@sec-retrieval) keeps
  retrieval from spending anchor slots on turns this step will attach anyway.

**Effect.** Contiguity is the largest single hydration effect in the
ablation record. Switching it off costs 0.06 to 0.09 packet gold-turn recall
(@sec-experimental). The round-3 ablation found the earlier 6 KiB budget and
lag-2 cap (top 6 anchors) binding. Raising the budget to 12 KiB and giving
every anchor lag-2 turns raised packet recall from 0.642 to 0.691 on
LongMemEval-S and from 0.597 to 0.629 on Eval 1, with 13 cases better and
none worse. Haiku-judged sufficiency rose by +0.048 ± 0.056 and
+0.037 ± 0.019, for +2.2 KB per Eval 1 packet. Budgets of 16 and 24 KiB gave
packets identical to 12 KiB. Clipping neighbours to 240 bytes raised a
clipped-text recall proxy but not judged sufficiency, so the clip stays at
480 bytes.

## Superseded-Predecessor and Superseding-Successor Hydration

At write time each new memory gets directed `supersedes` edges to the few
older memories whose embeddings fall in a knob-derived similarity band, and
the edge weight grows with similarity (@sec-advanced). These edges are
topical, not only corrections. Retrieval does not demote either endpoint.
Hydration uses the edges in both directions:

* **Predecessors.** For each of the top 11 anchors, the at most 2 older
  memories it supersedes (strongest edges first) are attached *before* the
  anchor's own content. Each is clipped to 512 bytes, under 4 KiB per packet.
  People do not lose the earlier version of a fact when they learn the newer
  one. Recalling the update brings back the episode it updated, and in these
  conversations the "obsolete" turn is often exactly what the question asks
  about.
* **Successors.** For each of the top 11 anchors, the newest memory that
  supersedes it is attached *after* its content. It is clipped to 512 bytes,
  under 4 KiB per packet, with one indexed lookup on the edge target for all
  anchors. A question phrased like a fact's first statement retrieves that
  older version, while the latest restatement ranks below it.

With both attachments, each anchor's evidence reads oldest to newest.

**Effect.** Switching off supersession edges and predecessor hydration
together changed 47/48 LongMemEval-S and 249/250 Eval 1 packets and cost
0.037, 0.025 and 0.015 packet recall (S, Eval 1, BEAM). Haiku-judged
sufficiency moved −0.036 ± 0.052 (S) and −0.016 ± 0.013 (Eval 1)
(@sec-experimental). Predecessor hydration used to skip a target from the
anchor's own source stream within 30 minutes. Removing that skip raised
BEAM-10M conversation 7 recall from 0.103 to 0.118 for 0.5 KB more packet
(@sec-advanced). Successor hydration added 0.005 gold-turn share at each BEAM
scale and +0.023 [0.010, 0.036] to the Haiku-answered 10M score
(@sec-implementation).

With `as_of`, both attachments and contiguity skip memories that start after
$T_q$.

## Per-Blob Content Timestamps

Attached blobs can come from weeks earlier (predecessors), from later
(successors), or from adjacent turns. The anchor's single `timestamp` does not
date them. Every retrieved memory therefore carries one stored signal time per
content blob, in content order, with 0 meaning unknown (PR #30).

* **Invariant.** Whenever `content` is non-empty,
  `content_timestamps.size() == content.size()`.
* **Coverage.** Every path that builds or reshapes content carries the source
  signal's time: signal and memory blob hydration, working-memory hydration,
  contiguity, predecessor and successor attachment, standing joins, and
  evidence fitting.
* **Modality.** Time stays signal metadata, never content.

**Known limit.** A multi-signal blob, such as a Natural unit's joined text,
reports the time of its first signal.

**Parity.** No ranking, selection, hydration choice or budget changed. Full
LoCoMo (1,986 queries) returned byte-identical text with 80,422 parts, none
with timestamp 0.

## Evidence Budget

The engine cannot know a reader's context budget, so the caller may pass one
per query in bytes (`EvidenceBudget`, on every `Process*` call and in the C
API). Text is charged by its bytes and every other payload by
`kMediaEvidenceBytes` = 480. Unset, memories come back whole. Earlier builds
applied a fixed 3 KiB cap per memory, which cost judged Eval 1 sufficiency
−0.016 ± 0.016 when the reader could see the whole packet.

Set, the fit runs once the packet is complete. It covers the standing block,
the retrieved memories and their attachments:

```text
budget' = budget - bytes(standing block)
for m in retrieved, in rank order:
    floor(m) = for a grouped memory whose members all have stored vectors:
                 its best member per modality by cos(e_q, v_s);
               otherwise: the whole memory
    join m at floor(m) with its attached blobs if they fit,
    else at floor(m) alone, else leave m out
member_cap = largest c (binary search) such that the packet fits when
             every grouped memory keeps its floor plus its other members,
             best first, while their bytes stay within c
kept members return in their original order, between the attachments
```

The best member is chosen per modality because cosines are not comparable
across modalities: a text query sits closer to every text member than to any
image. The fit keeps more distinct memories trimmed before it drops
lower-ranked ones. It costs one indexed signal read plus member payload reads,
and only for packets over budget.

**Effect.** Under Natural retention with one source per conversation, BEAM
stores units of three to five turns, about 10 KB each with attachments. An
8,000-token budget then held three or four whole memories. With the BEAM
reader's budget passed (34,800 bytes), the gold-turn share of its context
matched the old 3 KiB cap (−0.002 / +0.001 / +0.002 at 100K / 1M / 10M). The
end-to-end score was 0.842 / 0.806 / 0.715 against 0.844 / 0.811 / 0.695.
Unset, the whole memories overflow that reader, and gold share falls by
0.144 / 0.115 / 0.093 (@sec-implementation). Every v5 benchmark in
@sec-experimental runs at the 34,800-byte budget.
